2The test, in plain words

The test checks that the new texts lead the coordinator to the right choice. The coordinator is the session that plans the work and runs the agents.

  1. Four cases. Each is a case that a planner or a worker could bring to the coordinator. A planner is the agent that drafts a batch of work; a worker builds one piece of it. The cases were written before the new texts existed, so that the old texts lead the wrong way.
  2. Three readers. Two agents each acted as the coordinator, on a copy of the repository without the review. One had the old texts, the other the new ones. A third agent graded both answers without knowing which reader had which texts. Each case scores 3 points: 2 for the decision, 1 for the sources cited.
  3. The result. The new texts: 12 of 12. The old texts: 10 of 12. Both readers cited their sources in full. The old texts lost one point of decision in each of two cases.
  4. Where the old texts misled: the order traits' self type. The order traits are the library's traits for comparing values. Their self type stands for the type that implements the trait. A planner proposed to copy the compiler's prelude's spelling of it, comprises T, into the one library, as "the team's later word". The compiler's prelude is the compiler's own small library. The one library is the interpreter's, which both paths are to use. The reader with the old texts dropped the copy, which was right, but on a weaker ground: the library's own practice. And it kept the copy open, for a probe, a small experiment, and a question to you. It had the dates: Naden's text of 31 August 2012 is later than Steele's prelude edits of 5 and 6 June 2012. But no old text made the date decide. The new later-word and one-library entries do.
  5. Where the old texts misled: System on the compiled path. System is the library part that gives a program its arguments and its environment. A planner proposed to keep the compiler's own System, CompilerSystem, on the compiled path after the switch-over. The switch-over is the point where the compiled path moves onto the one library and the compiler's prelude is deleted. The reader with the old texts refused, but offered a CompilerSystem bridge as one option of a question to you. The old one-library entry gives no reason for one library. The new one gives yours: the switch-over exists so that walk's library, the interpreter's, is not ported into the compiler's.
  6. The other two cases. A worker offered to make a defect of the code generator a rule of the language. Another offered to fix a checker defect by copying a range trait from the compiler's prelude into the one library. In both cases, both readers chose right.

The test checks that the new texts lead the coordinator to the right choice. The coordinator is the session that plans the work and runs the agents.

  1. Four cases. Each is a case that a planner or a worker could bring to the coordinator. A planner is the agent that drafts a batch of work; a worker builds one piece of it. The cases were written before the new texts existed, so that the old texts lead the wrong way.
  2. Three readers. Two agents each acted as the coordinator, on a copy of the repository without the review. One had the old texts, the other the new ones. The reader with the old texts refused, but offered a CompilerSystem bridge as one option of a question to you. The old one-library entry gives no reason for one library. The new one gives yours: the switch-over exists so that walk's library, the interpreter's, is not ported into the compiler's.

content.content:
2The test, in plain words

The test checks that the new texts lead the coordinator to the right choice. The coordinator is the session that plans the work and runs the agents.


Four cases. Each is a case that a planner or a worker could bring to the coordinator. A planner is the agent that drafts a batch of work; a worker builds one piece of it. The cases were written before the new texts existed, so that the old texts lead the wrong way.

Three readers. Two agents each acted as the coordinator, on a copy of the repository without the review. One had the old texts, the other the new ones. A third agent graded both answers without knowing which reader had which texts. Each case scores 3 points: 2 for the decision, 1 for the sources cited.

The result. The new texts: 12 of 12. The old texts: 10 of 12. Both readers cited their sources in full. The old texts lost one point of decision in each of two cases.

Where the old texts misled: the order traits' self type. The order traits are the library's traits for comparing values. Their self type stands for the type that implements the trait. A planner proposed to copy the compiler's prelude's spelling of it, comprises T, into the one library, as "the team's later word". The compiler's prelude is the compiler's own small library. The one library is the library of walk, the interpreter; both paths are to use it. The reader with the old texts dropped the copy, which was right, but on a weaker ground: the library's own practice. And it kept the copy open, to be tested by a probe and then put to you as a question. A probe is a small experiment. It had the dates: Naden's text of 31 August 2012 is later than Steele's prelude edits of 5 and 6 June 2012. But no old text made the date decide. The new later-word and one-library entries do.

Where the old texts misled: System on the compiled path. System is the component, the part of the library, that gives a program its arguments and its environment. A planner proposed to keep the compiler's own System, CompilerSystem, on the compiled path after the switch-over. The switch-over is the point where the compiled path moves onto the one library and the compiler's prelude is deleted. The reader with the old texts refused, but offered a CompilerSystem bridge as one option of a question to you. The old one-library entry gives no reason for one library. The new one gives yours: the switch-over exists so that walk's library is not ported into the compiler's.

The other two cases. A worker offered to make a defect of the code generator a rule of the language. Another offered to fix a checker defect by copying a range trait from the compiler's prelude into the one library. In both cases, both readers chose right. 
---
3The answers these texts assume

Four of your answers are still open. The texts are written under the default of each. If you answer another way, the texts change as each point says.


Phase 3 closes with climb batch 22c, over fourteen components. Phase 3 is the work that makes the type checker accept the library's core components without error. A component is one part of the library, such as List. A climb batch is one run of the workflow in which agents build a set of rungs; a rung is one piece of work. The distance stage is the tool that counts the checker's errors over the library's twelve core components. The fourteen are those twelve, plus the two that List imports. Default: yes. If no: the one-library and phases entries count the twelve, not the fourteen, and the phases entry counts 40 other components, not 38.

The 38 other components block a later step, not the switch-over. The later step is the one at which walk, the interpreter, runs the checker on its programs, after the switch-over. Each component is cleared before that step, or before the first program that needs it. The judgement wrote 40, but two of the 40 are List's imports, which phase 3 now counts. Default: yes. If no: the one-library and phases entries say that the switch-over also needs those components to pass the checker and the code generator, and the entry on walk and the checker says they are cleared by then.

Three one-word answers. Defaults: drop "functions" from what the bound's entry says Any holds; strike the sentence "The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text." from the later-word entry; move the flat-numbers entry's two "Why" sentences to the record's history, the file that keeps each entry's earlier texts. If you keep any of these, that entry keeps its old words: the bound's entry says "tuples, functions and ()"; the later-word entry keeps the sentence; the flat-numbers entry keeps its two sentences and drops the one that calls the prelude's flat numbers "not a ground".

Your lean toward the class loader, recorded as a lean to confirm. On 20 September you leaned toward the class loader as the way to give an RR64 array, made through the library's generic array traits, a Java double[] store. The class loader is the part of the compiled path that makes Java classes while a program runs. Default: record it. If no: the array-questions entry drops its new sentence, and the array-store entry drops its last clause, which points to the lean. 
---
4.4The default bound is Any


"Functions" is dropped from what Any holds, under your open answer. The team's texts disagree on functions and agree on tuples. The title, your decision, is unchanged.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the grounds in the language. The 2019 paper says the default bound is Any. The Working Draft says type parameters take tuple types, which its own Object sentence would forbid, and that sentence isn't in the 2008 release. The library fills its type parameters with tuples, as zip does.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: Steele's 2012 setting enforces the draft's sentence on the compiled path alone; it is not the language's rule. The old text said the switch-over ends the Object bound. It doesn't: one line of Shell.java does. Under that line, some calls also compile wrong.

New: two failures of the compiled path that don't depend on the bound: () as a static argument, the type that fills a type parameter, and a generic method, called with a dot, whose one parameter has a tuple type. And, from the judgement, for your yes: Java gives no ground for Object, since Java's own Object maps to Fortress Any.


The new text 
---
4.5The phases of the work


New, from the judgement, for your yes: the order's ground is in the team's build. The compiled path runs the checker first, then code generation and the run time. The natives, the library functions whose body is Java, define the switch-over.

Phase 3's exit changes, from "no error on the interpreter's whole library" to no error and no crash over the fourteen components. It counts only under the compile command's own setting, with the bound Any, and with the export check reading operators and abstract members. The export check is the checker's test that each component provides what its api, its interface, lists. You agreed that "whole" was wrong. The new exit restates one that you approved, so it is yours to confirm: it is your open answer on phase 3.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the switch-over needs two zeros over the fourteen. Phase 3 brings the checker's; phase 4 brings the code generator's. The code generator's half was unmeasured when you approved the order; it now refuses 52 declarations.

New, from the judgement, for your yes, under your open answer: the 38 other components don't block the switch-over. Each is cleared before walk runs the checker, or before the first program that needs it.

The rest is the old text: phases 4 to 6, code-generator work beside that order, and the row on an api implemented by a component of another name.


The new text 
---
4.12The natives' form


A native binding is the body of a library function whose work is done in Java. It is written builtinPrimitive("…"), with a string that names the Java code. A helper is a static Java method that the compiled path can call. The decision is unchanged.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the ground. The language has no foreign-function interface; the Working Draft lists one only among proposed features. So the form of a binding belongs to Java interoperability, and the library's own practice decides it: every binding in the library is a builtinPrimitive call.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the specification prints builtinPrimitive only inside the library api that it includes, whose comment describes walk's way. That is no ground. The entry's first text gave it as one; this sentence keeps it from coming back.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the choice is cheap to undo only until the bindings start to move onto helpers. After that, the other form costs a pass over the whole library.

Your informed yes to this decision is still owed, before climb batch 23. An entry states no status, so the text doesn't say it.


The new text 
---
4.13Abstract members are declared in the component


A component's api lists what the component provides. A member that the api writes abstract must be declared in the component. The decision is unchanged.

Your reason stays yours, now headed "Why": by the team's later word, you prefer the compiled path's way to the interpreter's library's. The old label of the compiler's prelude as "the team's later work" is dropped, since the later-word entry now dates code against the texts.

New, from the judgement, for your yes: the ground. The specification's text is unclear: one section asks for no body and is silent on the declaration; another reads either way. Where the text is silent or unclear, the team's checker, which enforced the rule, is the team's own reading, and it binds. The failure at run time without the declaration is the cost of the other reading, not the ground.

The old words "the team's export check of 2012" become "the team's export check, in their tree by 2011-12". The git history shows the check only in imported snapshots with no parent commit, so its author and year can't be recovered.


The new text 
---

**Sentences in the sources that seem wrong or did not render plainly:**
1. **Answer 1 no longer changes any text.** The proposals list the "Still to build" line of P-42 and P-33 as text that depends on answer 1, but the coordinator cut those lines in `combined.apply`. So for P-42, answer 1 now changes nothing. For P-33, "the state line is dropped" is already true. Section 3 states only the changes that still apply.
2. **The judgement's count is inconsistent.** Its sections 1, 5 and 7 say "thirteen" components; the rewrite corrects this to fourteen. Its tenet 8 also gives 424 bindings in one sentence and 449 in the next. The page uses neither number.
3. **P-12 and P-33 count the other components differently.** P-12's new text says "F-290 counts 624 errors in the 40 components outside the twelve". F-290 itself says those errors fall in 30 of the 40. And P-33 says 38 outside the fourteen. Both are correct as written, but a reader may see a clash.
4. **The P-158 date has a weak source.** P-158 dates the export check only by imported snapshots with no parent commit. The page says its author and year cannot be recovered, as chunk one's proposals do.
5. **Words I chose:**
   - "component" for the texts' library parts, defined in section 2 and again in section 3.
   - "walk" for the interpreter.
   - "silent or unclear" for the texts' "silent or ambiguous".
